answer:
HYPOTHESIS (natural-language answer to "How did urban land use affect the invasion of different types of introduced plants?"):

Urban land use did not simply raise the number of invading introduced plants — it changed WHICH types of introductions invade. Regionally, the introduction pool itself shifted dramatically with the urbanization era: AgriForest introductions fell from 51% of the pool (Before 1500) to 6% (1985–2019), while Gardening introductions rose from 17% to 75% (χ² = 230.4, p < 1e-46). Locally in Barcelona province, plots surrounded by more urban land cover harbour roughly 25% more invader species per SD of urban cover (significant at all buffer radii), and plots above the median urban cover (1000 m) carry ~6× more invaders than low-urban plots (1.34 vs 0.21 species/plot). Crucially, progressive landscape change between 1956 and 2009 (urban+cropland expansion) did not change total invader richness, but it shifted the composition of the invader community: gardening-origin invaders were disproportionately represented in progressively changed landscapes (rate ratio 1.18 per SD of expansion, p = 0.003), whereas unintentionally introduced invaders were associated with high current urban cover (RR 1.12, p = 0.047) but were under-represented where recent expansion occurred (RR 0.89, p = 0.022) — consistent with a filter in which ornamental plants track actively urbanizing land, while accidental invaders accumulate in long-established (pre-existing) urban and cropland contexts. AgriForest invaders were rare (23 of 481 plot records) and trended away from urbanized plots (RR 0.54, n.s. — low power). At the species level, unintentionally introduced species achieve broader invaded niches (median 0.87 vs 0.36 for gardening species, KW p = 0.052) and occupy more plots than gardening species (NB coefficient +0.67, p = 0.013) after accounting for residence time (mrt +0.36 per SD, p = 0.005). Phylogenetically, introduction pathway is clustered on the tree (same-pathway species are more closely related than random: mean within-pathway distance 234.6 vs 246.2 permuted null, p < 0.002), but invasion success itself shows no phylogenetic signal (Pagel's λ ≈ 0.12, p = 0.71; λ = 0 for niche breadth and residence time) — so the urban–pathway associations are not artefacts of shared ancestry, and PGLS correction was unnecessary. In short: urbanization converted the region's invasion profile from an agriculture/forestry-driven one into a gardening-driven one, with actively expanding (urbanized or cropland-converted) landscapes preferentially invaded by ornamental introductions and established urban cores additionally accumulating accidentally introduced, broad-niche species.

WORKFLOW (executed): (A) χ² test on the 4×3 period×pathway contingency table. (B1) Negative-binomial GLMs of per-plot total invader counts (n=632; 441 zero-plots) on urban 2009 cover, cropland 2009 cover, 1956–2009 progressive/regressive change proportions, plus elevation, climate and road/stream distances — run at all three buffer radii for sensitivity (1000 m primary). (B2) Among the 191 invaded plots, pathway-composition models (Poisson GLM with log(n.total) offset, HC1 robust SEs; binomial GLMs were discarded due to quasi-complete separation for Gardening/Unintentional). (B3) Habitat × urban-context contrasts. (B4) Moran's I permutation test on model residuals (5 km neighbourhood, 199 permutations). (C) Species-level (deduplicated to 77 by Scientific_name, keeping first pathway assignment of the 4 dual-pathway species) Kruskal–Wallis tests and NB model of number.of.invaded.plots ~ pathway + mrt with rotated references. (D) Manual Newick parsing (81 tips, 81/81 CSV match; 77 used after dedup), pairwise cophenetic distances, Pagel's λ via bounded MLE + LR tests, and a 999-permutation test of within-pathway phylogenetic distance; PGLS skipped because λ ≈ 0. (E) Synthesis of coefficients into the hypothesis above.

payload.hypothesis: Urban land use changed not just how many introduced plants invade but which types: rising urban cover increases invader richness overall, and progressive urban+cropland expansion (1956–2009) shifts the invader community toward Gardening-origin (ornamental) introductions (RR 1.18, p=0.003), mirroring the regional historical shift from AgriForest-dominated (51% before 1500) to Gardening-dominated (75% in 1985–2019) introduction pools. Unintentional invaders concentrate in long-established high-urban contexts (urban cover RR 1.12, p=0.047; expansion RR 0.89, p=0.022) and have broader invaded niches and higher plot occupancy than gardening species after controlling for residence time; AgriForest introductions are rare, trend away from urban plots, and are underpowered. Pathway membership is phylogenetically clustered (p<0.002) but invasion success shows no phylogenetic signal (λ≈0.12, p=0.71), so the urban–pathway associations are not confounded by shared ancestry.
